blocks.text: The results of mechanical tests are usually expressed in terms of stress and strain, which are defined in terms of applied force and deformation.
It is defined as the force applied per unit area to produce any change in the shape, volume or length of a body. Mathematically, it is expressed as:

The SI unit of stress (σ) is newton per square meter (N m⁻²), which is given the name pascal (Pa). Stress may cause a change in length, volume and shape. When a stress changes length, it is called the tensile stress, when it changes the volume, it is called the volume stress and when it changes the shape, it is called the shear stress.

Strain is a measure of the deformation of a solid when stress is applied to it. In the case of deformation in one dimension, strain is defined as the fractional change in length. If ΔL is the change in length and L₀ is the original length (Fig. 5.3 (a), then strain is given by

blocks.text_alt: Strain (ε) = Change in length (ΔL) / Original length (L₀)   (5.2)

blocks.alt: A pink bar of length L is pulled by a force F at each end, the arrows pointing outward. Dotted outlines beyond both ends show how far the bar is stretched.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.3(a): Tensile strain (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.3(a)).

blocks.text: Since strain is the ratio of lengths, it is dimensionless and therefore, has no units. If strain ε is due to tensile stress σ, it is called tensile strain, and if it is produced as a result of compressive stress σ, it is termed as compressive strain.

blocks.title: Young's modulus
blocks.text: The stress applied per unit strain is called Young's modulus

blocks.text_alt: i.e. Y = Tensile stress / Tensile strain

blocks.text: It has the same unit as that of stress i.e., N m⁻² or Pa. The value of Young's modulus of different material is given in Table 5.1.
There are various methods to determine the Young's modulus of a wire. One of the method is Searle's method.

blocks.title: For Your Information
blocks.text: Although it is named after the 19th century British Scientist Thames Young, the concept was developed in 1727 by Leonhard Euller.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The names are misprinted: the British scientist is Thomas Young (1773–1829), and the mathematician is Leonhard Euler.
